newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open up as overseas shorts covered.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open up as overseas shorts covered.

text.p: The prices of U.S. government securities were expected to improve from already higher levels reached in overnight trade in London Friday.

Thursday the yield on the 30-year bond jumped to its highest level since October following the release of news pointing to a healthy manufacturing sector. It opened up 7/32 at 97-5/32 to yield 6.72 percent on Friday.
London's overnight session was highlighted by short-covering among dealers and that pattern of activity was expected to continue in New York.
"We saw a lot of short-covering in London overnight and that's likely to follow through in the New York trading session," said Kevin Flanagan, money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.
Flanagan said many bottom-fishers would be in the market Friday and traders were awaiting the release of November construction spending at 1000 EST/1500 GMT.
Also slated for release throughout the trading session were U.S. auto and light truck sales.
Traders noted that volume has been unusually heavy for a holiday-shortened week and could pick up even more Monday.

Also helping to bolster the market was a strong U.S. dollar, which gained again in European trading. The dollar has done particularly well against the Japanese yen recently, though there was no trade in Tokyo overnight as New Year holidays continued.

Bond market participants said the specter of higher interest rates has spooked the market in recent days. The Federal Reserve's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee next meets to decide the fate of short-term rates on Feb. 4 and 5. Higher interest rates deflate the value of fixed-income securities.

"The market's basically stabilized in early trading after the last two days of heavy losses. The dollar's doing better and that's also helping," said James Blumenthal, bond market analyst at MCM Moneywatch. He expected a fairly quiet session.
Ten-year notes were up 3/32 to 99-31/32, yielding 6.50 percent. Five-year notes were up 2/32 to 99-12/32, yielding 6.27 percent. Two-year notes were up 1/32 at 99-21/32, yielding 5.94 percent.
